\section{Resistance and Ohm's Law}

The voltage tells us how much energy each coulomb can give up; the current tells us how quickly charge is moving. We still need a rule connecting the electrical ``push'' to the resulting flow through a component. For a component at a particular operating point, define its resistance by
\[
\boxed{R=\frac{V}{I}},\qquad \boxed{V=IR},\qquad \boxed{I=\frac{V}{R}}.
\]
Resistance is measured in ohms ($\Omega$), where $1\,\Omega=1\,\mathrm{V/A}$. A larger resistance means less current for the same p.d.; a larger p.d. means more current for the same resistance.

\myskip
\textbf{Ohm's law.} An ohmic component at constant temperature has a constant resistance, so its p.d. is directly proportional to its current:
\[
\boxed{V\propto I\quad\text{and hence}\quad V=IR\text{ with constant }R.}
\]
The phrase ``at constant temperature'' matters. A metal filament heats as current increases, changing its resistance, so a filament lamp is non-ohmic. For a non-ohmic component, $V/I$ is still its resistance at that operating point, but it is not a single constant for all currents.

A $V$--$I$ graph makes the distinction visible: a straight line through the origin represents an ohmic component, and its slope is $R$. A curve represents a resistance that changes with operating conditions. This is why the formula is useful, but should not be applied blindly to every device.

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Question.} A voltage of $1.5$ V is applied across a $2\,\Omega$ lamp. What current would flow if its resistance at that operating point is $2\,\Omega$?

\textbf{Solution.} The known quantities are $V$ and $R$, so use $I=V/R$:
\[
I=\frac{1.5}{2}=\boxed{0.75\text{ A}}.
\]
The answer is an operating-point calculation; it does not claim that a real lamp keeps $R=2\,\Omega$ as it heats.
\end{exercise}

\myskip
\textbf{How to attack a difficult circuit problem.} A complicated drawing becomes manageable when each law is used for the job it describes. Use this order:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*:},itemsep=3pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item Mark the current direction (or choose one temporarily) and identify the source p.d. or net emf.
  \item Mark junctions and nodes. In one unbranched path the current is the same; at a junction, currents split and recombine.
  \item Identify the p.d. across each component. Parallel branches share the same p.d.; a resistor's drop is $V_R=IR$.
  \item Write one equation for each useful loop or junction, then solve for the requested quantity.
  \item Check the result: voltage rises equal drops around a loop, junction currents balance, and a negative current means the true direction is opposite to the choice.
\end{enumerate}
This separation prevents a common error: using the same-current rule in a parallel branch, or using the same-voltage rule for components that are actually in series.

\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Question.} A $6$ V battery is connected to $1\,\Omega$ and $3\,\Omega$ resistors in series. Find the current through the $3\,\Omega$ resistor.

\textbf{Solution.} There is only one path, so the current is the same through both resistors. The total resistance is $1+3=4\,\Omega$, and therefore
\[
I=\frac{6}{4}=\boxed{1.5\text{ A}}.
\]
The $3\,\Omega$ resistor carries this same $1.5$ A, not $6/3=2$ A: it does not receive the full battery p.d. The drops are $1.5$ V and $4.5$ V, which add to $6$ V.
\end{exercise}

\myskip
\begin{exercise}
\textbf{Question.} Three identical resistors are connected first in series and then in parallel to the same $6$ V battery. If the total power in series is $x$ and in parallel is $y$, find $x:y$.

\textbf{Solution.} Let each resistance be $R$. In series, $R_s=3R$, while in parallel $R_p=R/3$. For the same battery voltage, use $P=V^2/R$:
\[
x=\frac{V^2}{3R},\qquad y=\frac{V^2}{R/3}=\frac{3V^2}{R}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{x:y=1:9}.
\]
The check is physical as well as algebraic: parallel gives three separate paths and a smaller total resistance, so it draws more current and power from an ideal source.
\end{exercise}

\textbf{Equipotential wires: the colouring method.} A plain piece of wire (and, ideally, a closed switch or an ammeter) has \emph{no} component in it, so there is no p.d. across it: both ends sit at exactly the same potential. This gives a fast, reliable way to read any circuit:

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,topsep=3pt]
  \item Start at one terminal. Follow \emph{every} stretch of bare wire you can reach without crossing a resistor, lamp, cell, open switch, or other component. Continue around corners and into every side branch. Give this entire connected set one colour: it is one node at one potential.
  \item Stop the colour only at a component or a genuine break. Begin a new colour on the other side, then again follow that colour through all connected bare wires.
  \item At a crossing, look for a junction dot. A dot means the wires join and share one colour; no dot means one wire merely passes over the other, so the colours remain separate.
  \item Now read off the topology directly:
  \begin{itemize}[itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item Any two components joined to the \emph{same pair of colours} are in \textbf{parallel} (same p.d. across them).
    \item If a component has the \emph{same colour on both ends}, it is \textbf{short-circuited}: zero p.d., so it carries no current and can be ignored.
  \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Colour the whole node, not just the main rail.} If a branch is made only of wire until it reaches a component terminal, that branch wire belongs to the same node and must receive the same colour. Component bodies form the boundaries between colours.
